doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Bootlegging, piracy and the unissued Live in Tokyo Gil Evans recording
summary: Levin dislikes copying of music, and tells how his own tape of a late-70s Gil Evans Tokyo concert appeared as a bootleg CD no one authorized.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well let me ask you about that. As somebody who obviously writes a lot of music and records a lot, how do you feel about people taking your stuff for nothing?

Well I don’t like it obviously. It happens a lot in many ways. There’s the concept of bootlegging for instance has been going on for years, which is somebody just makes an illegal copy or an illegal recording or something. “Illegal” being without permission. And they distribute it or sometimes sell it, sometimes just pass it around. It seems innocent on a one-shot basis. But one way or another, to some degree, it’s costing some musician somewhere or a composer.

A dollar, or two dollars if it gets widespread enough. It definitely has an impact. And I think people don’t realize that it’s the same concept of the way people copy software and pass it around. Computer software. It doesn’t seem like a big — if you bought it and then make a copy for a friend or something, it doesn’t really feel like stealing. The people that do it are not thieves, they’re nice people. It’s hard to see the impact that it’s having on a whole industry when you do it. I had some help doing it but I contributed to it somewhere on my website there’s a discography of stuff that I’ve done or stuff that I can remember doing. Not that mine is — there are people with much bigger discographies, but there’s a lot of stuff on there. And as I traveled so many years with Gil Evans, especially in Europe, I started looking around to see what, okay, let’s get a list of the albums that Pete is on. And he showed me the list. And he said, “Wait a minute, what is this? I don’t have a copy of that. What is that?” And we looked and realized nobody had a copy of it and Gil didn’t even know about it. And we recorded a lot in situations where the band didn’t know we were being recorded. There was one great concert in the late 70s in Tokyo. It was I think still my favorite concert that I ever played with Gil Evans, for a lot of reasons — opening up a whole other story. Shortening it I had that particular day, it was in Tokyo, and I had just bought a brand new tape recorder which was my souvenir from Japan because they were cheaper there at the time. I don’t think it matters anymore, but it was a kind of a cutting edge portable deck. And I bought it to the gig and borrowed a couple of microphones from the sound guys, and I said I’ll just record the concert for the hell of it. And it was this amazing concert. And years later I took it back and transferred it to a multi-track tape, because there were some problems with it. For some reason I had no bass on it at all. And I actually brought Jeff Berlin in, the original bass player, into the studio. And Jeff is one of these — he’s a very creative guy but he thinks like a machine. I mean if you play something once, he could, in ten years, play it note for note the same way. So I brought Jeff in and I had him replace all his bass parts, you know, playing along with it. And I kind of mastered it a little bit at a time. And then I put it together as a project. I gave Gil a copy of it, and he was thrilled because he had liked the concert too. And I talked to him about it, said you know I should get this to a record company and maybe we could issue it. And I think a few weeks later I had actually played it for some

record people to see if I could get some interest going. It was a little shaky. It was not great quality because it was a live recording and there were flaws, but it was nice, it was a really nice set. A few weeks later I was in Tower Records and just thumbing through some bins and I pull out a CD “Live in Tokyo.” Hello? We never made any record like that. And I looked at it and I looked at the personnel and the pictures and the songs. They were the same. That was the concert. We have no idea who recorded it. I tried to track it down. It was an Italian record company, a Japanese production. Somebody probably taping off the board while we did it. And then they just issued it. Gil didn’t know about it. Nobody got paid obviously. So much for my big production of a Gil Evans album.

So again I’m going on the long way, but it’s eventually evolved into a publicly perceived perception or an attitude that any music that you see out there, it’s okay to just take it. And again it’s not being done by people who are inherently thieves or bad people, it’s just kind of a prevailing attitude.
